results.text:
Imagine navigating a supermarket where every aisle looks almost identical.

The shelves repeat, the corridors look similar, and after walking through aisle after aisle, small positioning errors can accumulate. Over time, the map of where you've been can gradually drift out of alignment.

That's exactly the kind of challenge LingBot-Map 2.0 is designed to address.

LingBot-Map 2.0 builds a 3D map from ordinary video while the camera is still moving. Its key upgrade is Refine: a step that can be triggered at any time to go back and revise the model's spatial memory, reducing accumulated drift entirely inside the model, without an external optimization backend.

In the supermarket demo, orange shows the camera's estimated path before Refine, while cyan shows the corrected path afterward. Both are from LingBot-Map 2.0.

This ability to revisit and correct spatial memory is crucial for robots navigating large, repetitive environments over long periods.

LingBot-Map 2.0 is a key ability of the embodied-native, general-purpose robot brain @robbyant_brain is building. Without reliable spatial memory, there's no autonomous work over large areas and long hours

results.text:
Imagine a robot navigating a pharmacy during the night shift...

On its first task, it has to search through the aisles to locate a particular shelf. Later, it's asked to navigate to another location it has already seen in the same pharmacy.

Instead of searching from scratch, it can reuse the spatial memory built during earlier tasks, making navigation faster in areas it has already explored.

That's the idea behind LingBot-Navi.

LingBot-Navi keeps spatial memory across tasks. The more it works in the same place, the faster it can locate targets and navigate through areas it already knows.
It came out back to back with LingBot-Map 2.0.

LingBot-Map 2.0 builds and corrects spatial memory, and LingBot-Navi uses that memory to find targets and navigate. Navi also keeps spatial memory after a task ends, so the next task in the same pharmacy can build on what the robot has already seen.

Together, they connect spatial perception, memory updates, and navigation, filling in key abilities for the embodied-native, general-purpose robot brain Robbyant is building.

LingBot-Navi is open source, including its model weights. @robbyant_brain

results.text:
Another European car factory starts training a humanoid worker…

Volvo Cars is training Hexagon Robotics’ AEON at its Ghent factory in Belgium. AEON uses a wheel-legged design, stands 1.65 m tall, weighs 60 kg, and can carry up to 10 kg at speeds of up to 2.4 m/s.

AEON has also been tested at BMW’s Leipzig plant, with further manufacturing collaborations involving Schaeffler and Fill Maschinenbau. It is designed to fit into existing production environments, working alongside employees and factory automation without major infrastructure changes.

At Volvo, AEON is learning through imitation learning, starting with precisely placing components into two fixtures. Further training will cover more parts-handling tasks and interaction with existing factory automation.

Volvo plans to expand the program in the first half of 2027, targeting a production pilot by mid-2027.

Replace humans with humanoid robots for high-risk tasks...

EngineAI’s a promotional video showcases a whole-body teleoperation platform for humanoid robots.

By wearing a VR headset and motion-capture gloves, a human operator can control a T800 humanoid  to perform tasks that are high-risk, dirty, strenuous, or physically demanding--such as handling medical waste, inspecting electrical substations, spray painting... even providing remote care for elderly individuals living at home.

Teleoperation serves both as a method for collecting real-world data and as a hybrid solution (keeping a human in the loop, though the ultimate goal is full autonomy).

Let’s look at how it performs in reality.

results.text:
A humanoid care robot lifts a bedridden "patient."

Waseda, University of Edinburgh, Abu Dhabi’s TII and partners trained Waseda’s AIREC (35 DoF, omnidirectional base, non-bipedal) with reinforcement learning in simulation, then open-loop replayed the learned trajectories on the real robot.

In a bedroom scene, AIREC transferred a 155 cm, 15 kg clothed medical mannequin from nursing bed to wheelchair without any human assistance.

The authors note this shows physical feasibility, but it is not a full closed-loop hardware validation--the same trajectory does not always succeed. The mannequin’s wrists and knees were loosely bound to reduce difficulty; current shoulder torque is still insufficient for a ~50 kg real person.

Strategy is feasible. With further hardware optimization, i think,AIREC could become a capable humanoid caregiver.
